Opiz }} }} '''''Lamium purpureum''''' (from Latin {{lang|la|purpureus}} {{gloss|[[purple]]}}), known as '''red dead-nettle''',{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}} '''purple dead-nettle''', or '''purple archangel''',[[Martin, W. Keble]], 1965. ''The Concise British Flora in Colour.'' George Rainbird Limited. is an annual herbaceous [[flowering plant]] in the mint family ([[Lamiaceae]]). It is native to Eurasia but can also be found in North America. ==Description== ''Lamium purpureum'' grows with square stems to {{Convert|5–20|cm|frac=2}},Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}} rarely {{Convert|40|cm|abbr=on}}, in height.{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=49}} The [[leaves]] have fine [[Trichome|hairs]], are green at the bottom and shade to purplish at the top; they are {{Convert|2–4|cm|frac=4}} long and broad, with a {{Convert|1-2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] (leaf stalk), and wavy to serrated margins. The [[zygomorphic]] flowers are bright red-purple, with the five petals fused into a corolla tube with a top hood-like lobe, two lower lip lobes and minute fang-like lobes between. This encloses the four stamens and the single style with its forked stigma. The [[Petal|corolla]] shows a line of hairs near the base of the tube. They may be produced throughout the year, including mild weather in winter. ===Phytochemistry=== The essential oil is characterized by its high contents of [[germacrene D]].{{Cite journal | last1 = Flamini | first1 = G. | last2 = Cioni | first2 = P. L. | last3 = Morelli | first3 = I. | title = Composition of the essential oils and in vivo emission of volatiles of four Lamium species from Italy: L. Purpureum, L. Hybridum, L. Bifidum and L. Amplexicaule | doi = 10.1016/j.foodchem.2004.05.047 | journal = Food Chemistry | volume = 91 | pages = 63–68 | year = 2005 }} The seed oil contains 16% of an acid characterized as (−)-octadeca-5,6-trans-16-trienoic acid (trivial name [[lamenallenic acid]]). Other unsaturated esters identified by their cleavage products are [[oleate]], [[linoleate]] and [[linolenate]].{{Cite journal|pmc=1198447|year=1967|last1=Mikolajczak|first1=KL|last2=Rogers|first2=MF|last3=Smith Cr|first3=Jun|last4=Wolff|first4=I. A.|title=An octadecatrienoic acid from Lamium purpureum L. Seed oil containing 5,6-allenic and trans-16-olefinic unsaturation|volume=105|issue=3|pages=1245–1249|journal=Biochemical Journal|pmid=16742552|doi=10.1042/bj1051245}} The plant contains [[phenylethanoid]] glycosides named lamiusides A, B, C, D and E.{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1248/cpb.54.1705 | last1 = Ito | first1 = N. | last2 = Nihei | first2 = T. | last3 = Kakuda | first3 = R. | last4 = Yaoita | first4 = Y. | last5 = Kikuchi | first5 = M. | title = Five new phenylethanoid glycosides from the whole plants of Lamium purpureum L | journal = Chemical & Pharmaceutical Bulletin | volume = 54 | issue = 12 | pages = 1705–1708 | year = 2006 | pmid = 17139106 | doi-access = free }} It possesses a flavonol 3-O-glucoside-6″-O-malonyltransferase.{{Cite journal | last1 = Suzuki | first1 = H. | title = CDNA cloning and functional characterization of flavonol 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-malonyltransferases from flowers of Verbena hybrida and Lamium purpureum | doi = 10.1016/j.molcatb.2004.01.005 | journal = Journal of Molecular Catalysis B: Enzymatic | volume = 28 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 87–93| year = 2004 }} === Similar species === It is often found alongside [[henbit dead-nettle]] (''Lamium amplexicaule''), for which it is easily mistaken, because the two species bear not only similar leaves, but also similar bright purple flowers. They can, however, be distinguished from one another by the form of the leaves on their respective flowering stems: those of red dead-nettle are [[Petiole (botany)|petiolate]], while those of henbit dead-nettle are [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]]. Though superficially similar to species of ''[[Urtica]]'' (true nettles) in appearance, ''L. purpureum'' is not related to them, the genus ''[[Lamium]]'' belonging to the [[mint family]], not the [[nettle family]], the "dead" in the name "dead-nettle" referring to the inability of ''[[Lamium]]'' species to sting. ''L. purpureum'' is the [[type species]] in its genus[https://www.ipni.org/n/30027405-2 International Plant Names Index: ''Lamium'' L.] and family; species in other [[Lamioideae]] genera may also look similar, including ''[[Stachys]]'' the "hedge nettles". ==Taxonomy== ''Lamium purpureum'' was described and named by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.{{r|IPNI:448939-1}} It is the [[type species]] of genus ''Lamium''.{{sfnp|Mennema|1989|page=26}} [[File:Lamium purpureum leaf structure featuring trichomes.tif|thumb|Leaf Structure of purple dead-nettle highlighting trichomes. Winston-Salem, North Carolina]] [[File:Stem and Trichome Image of Lamium purpureum.tif|thumb|Cross-sectional cut of purple dead-nettle stem featuring trichome structures. Winston-Salem, North Carolina]] ==Distribution and habitat== ''Lamium purpureum'' is native and relatively common to Europe (including Britain and IrelandClapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}) and Asia but it can also be found in North America:{{Cite web |title=Lamium purpureum (Purple Archangel) - FSUS |author= |work=Flora of the Southeastern United States |publisher=[[North Carolina Botanical Garden]] |year=2025 |access-date=21 July 2025 |url= https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/show-taxon-detail.php?taxonid=5332}} especially in the western and eastern United States,{{Cite book|title=Weeds of the West|last=Whitson|first=Tom|publisher=Western Society of Weed Science in cooperation with the Western United States Land Grant Universities Cooperative Extension Services.|year=2000|isbn=9780788149269|location=Newark, California}} and Canada. It frequently occurs in meadows, forest edges, roadsides and gardens. ==Ecology== The year-round flowers allow [[bee]]s to gather their [[nectar]] for food when few other nectar sources are available. It is also a prominent source of [[pollen]] for bees in March/April (in UK), when bees need the pollen as protein to build up their nest.{{Citation needed|date=November 2024}} The pollen is crimson red in colour and thus very noticeable on the heads of the bees that visit its flowers.{{cite book |author=Dorothy Hodges |title=The pollen loads of the honeybee |publisher=Bee Research Association Ltd., London |year=1952}}https://michaelqpowell.com/2020/05/04/red-pollen/ Retrieved at 14.57 on Thursday 22 August 2024. ==Uses== Young plants have edible tops and leaves, which can be used in salads or stir-fried as a spring vegetable. When finely chopped, they can also be added to sauces.{{Cite web|title=Purple Deadnettle: Pictures, Flowers, Leaves & Identification {{!}} Lamium purpureum|url=https://www.ediblewildfood.com/purple-deadnettle.aspx|access-date=2021-04-17|website=www.ediblewildfood.com}} The flowers can be crystallized using sugar and [[egg white]]. The herb has a venerable pedigree in the [[Traditional medicine|folk medicine]] of England, featuring as it does as one of three medicinal/symbolic plants called for in the Anglo-Saxon herb charm [[Wið færstice]] {{IPA|ang|wið ˈfæːrˌsti.t͡ʃe|}} (meaning 'against a sudden/violent stabbing pain'). The charm in question (dating, according to scholarly consensus, probably from the late ninth century) calls for the three herbs involved (the other two being [[feverfew]] and [[Plantago|plantain]]) to be heated in butter to prepare an ointment, which is then rubbed on the site of the pain with the blade of a knife, while the lengthy charm is recited by the folk practitioner, who thereby aligns herself (or himself) with the patient – in contradistinction to the evil supernatural beings believed to have caused the pain with their magical arrows.{{cite book |last=Pollington |first=Stephen |title=Leechcraft: Early English Charms, Plantlore and Healing |year=2000 |publisher=Anglo-Saxon Books |isbn=978-1-898281-47-4}} To this day, herbalists use red dead-nettle in many herbal remedies. One of these is a salve prepared from the plant which can be used [[Topical medication|topically]] to soothe irritated, itchy, or sore skin.{{Cite web|title=Wildcrafting Purple Dead Nettle For Food And Medicine|url=https://www.outdoorapothecary.com/purple-dead-nettle/|access-date=2021-03-23|website=www.outdoorapothecary.com|date=23 March 2021 }} Studies show a strong [[antioxidant]] effect.{{Cite journal |last1=Bubueanu |first1=Corina |last2=Gheorghe |first2=Campeanu |last3=Pirvu |first3=Lucia |last4=Bubueanu |first4=George |date=5 September 2013 |title=ANTIOXIDANT ACTIVITY OF BUTANOLIC EXTRACTS OF ROMANIAN NATIVE SPECIES -Lamium album AND Lamium purpureum |journal=Romanian Biotechnological Letters |volume=18 |issue=6 |pages=8861}} ==Gallery== File:Illustration Lamium purpureum0.jpg|1885 illustration File:Hoja SVG (Lamium purpureum).svg|Leaf detail File:Red Dead nettle close 700.jpg|[[Essex]], England,
